newsitem.title: USA: Merger of USDA farm agencies unlikely -- Glickman.
newsitem.headline: Merger of USDA farm agencies unlikely -- Glickman.

text.p: The Clinton administration is unlikely to propose merger of the U.S. agencies that run soil conservation and farm subsidy programs, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Wednesday.
"I would not look for any radical reorganization changes to be included in the final presidential budget message," Glickman said during an impromptu interview with Reuters.

"I think that they're going to continue to press for administrative reforms in the management of our agencies. But unitl it's done, you don't really know what's there, so I haven't been too frightened by those reports."

The White House budget office suggested merger of the two agencies in "pass-back" documents that were part of preparing the fiscal 1998 budget, according to a private-sector source. The administration will unveil its plan in early 1997.
Asked about the report, Glickman said, "There are always lots of ideas that go back and forth, back and forth" during drafting of the budget.

Merger of the two agencies was debated, and rejected, by lawmakers in 1994 when Congress passed a reorganization law. They said separate agencies were essential because of the profoundly different jobs they performed.
Environmentalists also opposed a merger on grounds soil erosion and water quality rules would not be aggressively enforced unless they were operated by conservationists.

Proponents said a merger made sense because most farmers had to do business with both agencies. The Farm Service Agency, which runs the farm subsidy program, was created from the Agricultural Stabilization and Conservation Service, and parts of Farmers Home Administration and crop insurance marketing.
Consolidation was intended to give farmers "one-stop shopping" and make efficient use of staff and office space.
